book: 027 - Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics

chapters.relation: Auxier frames Hitchcock's Lifeboat against Garrett Hardin's 'lifeboat ethics' essay, arguing the lifeboat converts political questions into ethical ones by stranding the survivors outside law and politics ('We're on our own here. We can make our own law'). The survivors are ethical pluralists - Rittenhouse lives for money, Kovac for equality, Constance for fame, Joe for God, MacKenzie for care - and their clinging to private versions of the Good lets Nazi captain Willy, whose only principle is survival, manipulate them all. Using Maslow's hierarchy of needs, Auxier shows the boat descending to bare survival, yet argues the mob killing of Willy when he hoards water is moral outrage rather than survival-driven, and that the final rescue scene replays the opening dispute with nobody having grown - a vindication of pluralistic democracy capable of unified action.

Sanders uses Bruno Anthony's 'criss-cross' murder-swap proposal to Guy Haines in Strangers on a Train to pose the classic question 'Why be moral?' to the charming amoralist. He tests three answers: Kant's categorical imperative fails because Bruno's egoist maxim ('remove obstacles to your happiness') can apparently be universalized; Hobbesian contractarian 'morality pays' fails because Bruno free-rides on others' restraint; and the Rachels/Nelson/Thomas psychological-health answer assumes rather than proves that Bruno should care about comparable suffering. A thought experiment comparing the moral life with the Bruno-state from an impartial standpoint leads to Aristotle's eudaimonia: morality is constitutive of human flourishing, so Bruno enjoys only a counterfeit happiness.

Silberstein reads Rear Window as a self-reflexive film about film-watching: the shades rise like a curtain, the courtyard apartments play like frames on a filmstrip, and wheelchair-bound Jeff with his binoculars is the movie spectator - the courtyard is Plato's cave and we are the chained prisoners watching shadows (copies of copies of the forms). The chapter stages the Plato-versus-Aristotle debate over imitative art from Republic Book X and the Poetics, then argues the film vindicates both: Jeff's voyeurism breeds detachment and misjudgment (he misreads Lisa, Miss Torso, the composer and the newlyweds), yet the same watching awakens - the song 'Lisa' saves Miss Lonelyhearts from suicide, Thorwald is brought to justice, and Jeff and the audience leave the theater wiser about fantasy, boredom and their own lives.

Skoble asks exactly what Jeff does wrong in Rear Window and whether his illicit snooping can generate genuine duties. Against a purely consequentialist verdict ('it all worked out okay'), he argues that knowledge creates conditional obligations - given what he has seen of Thorwald, Jeff's intervention is obligatory rather than supererogatory, by 'ought implies can' - and he weighs autonomy-respecting limits on intervening in Miss Lonelyhearts' despair. He then analyzes privacy as a moral right grounded in reciprocal legitimate expectations, concluding that Jeff violated no such right since everything he watched was on public display, so the ends-justify-the-means charge mostly dissolves.

chapters.file: ch26 - V - What’s It All About, Alfred.md

chapters.relation: Kinghorn asks what makes Hitchcock's trademark plot twists improbable, distinguishing physical, statistical and evidential probability and illustrating each with the fraying jacket seam in Saboteur, the sea of identical umbrellas in Foreign Correspondent, the porter uniforms in North by Northwest, and Manny Balestrero's uncanny double in The Wrong Man. The core of the chapter is a three-question method for assessing evidence - does the evidence fit the theory, does it fit rival theories too, how likely was the theory beforehand - worked out through Jeff and Doyle's debates over Thorwald's guilt in Rear Window, where Jeff turns out to be a methodologically sound amateur sleuth despite his bias against marriage. A closing lesson defends design-argument-style reasoning about God from a confused objection that demands statistics where only evidential probability is at issue.

Holt uses Hitchcock's cameo appearances - the Reduco newspaper ad in Lifeboat, the double-bass in Strangers on a Train, the wheelchair in Topaz - as a case study in theories of artistic interpretation. Joke and allusion cameos support Intentionalism, but the cameos began as a casting expediency in The Lodger and their significance arose before Hitchcock envisioned it, which troubles Intentionalism; the Where's-Waldo spotting game and the cameos' mundanity, which adds a touch of realism to the fictional world, give ground to New Criticism and a limited Subjectivism. He concludes that all three theories hold within their respective domains and that 'the' meaning of art is a false ideal - plural, constrained interpretation is the truth of the cameos.

The Deavels argue that Hitchcock's suspense is fundamentally epistemological. In the social world, heroines in love - Constance in Spellbound, Lina in Suspicion, Rose in The Wrong Man - must weigh mounting evidence of their beloveds' guilt against the Aristotelian premise that character is consistent because virtue and vice are habits: Constance rightly bets that J.B.'s gentleness with her proves he is no murderer, Lina reasonably concludes Johnnie may poison her, and Rose survives only by inventing a persecutory 'they'. With The Birds the question widens to nature itself: Mrs. Bundy's ornithology assumes past bird behavior predicts future behavior, and the film's terror is Hume's worry that causal order may be an unfounded projection, leaving Mitch to stake his family's escape on the humble observed pattern that attacks come in waves.

chapters.file: ch30 - Marnie An Enigma to Herself.md
chapters.relation: Yanal sets Descartes's two claims about mind - certainty about one's own thoughts (via the method of doubt and the deceiving-evil-genius possibility) and skepticism about other minds (hats and coats that may cover automata) - against Wittgenstein's counters, then reads Shadow of a Doubt and Marnie as Hitchcock's counterexamples. In Shadow of a Doubt the two Charlies, twins in blood and in the film's doubling motifs, are 'transparent' to each other - Young Charlie alone knows her uncle is the Merry Widow Murderer - refuting other-minds skepticism; in Marnie, repressed memory of killing her mother's sailor client leaves Marnie ignorant of her own mind until Mark's amateur therapy recovers it, refuting Cartesian self-certainty. Both films thus side with Wittgenstein: one person can know another's mind, and one can be an enigma to oneself.

holes.name: Ethical Pluralism
holes.what: The view that people legitimately embrace the same goals and moral order for different and often conflicting reasons, so a community can act together while holding diverse conceptions of the good life.
holes.why: Chapter 22 explicitly defines and defends ethical pluralism as its thesis about Lifeboat: each survivor's different version of the Good is preserved, and the boat's collective action springs from converging moral outrage rather than shared doctrine.

holes.name: Lifeboat Ethics (Hardin)
holes.what: Garrett Hardin's thought experiment picturing rich nations as passengers on a lifeboat who cannot take on more poor 'swimmers' without swamping everyone.
holes.why: Chapter 22 opens with and constantly returns to Hardin's essay, using the lifeboat scenario as a device that strips away politics and law to isolate ethical decision-making.

holes.name: Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs
holes.what: Abraham Maslow's theory that human motivation ascends a hierarchy from physiological and safety needs through love and esteem to self-actualization, with morality at the top.
holes.why: Chapter 22 devotes a full section to reading the Lifeboat survivors' descent to bare survival through the hierarchy, then argues Maslow 'loses the card game' because moral outrage overrides survival.

holes.name: Aristotle's Poetics (mimesis and catharsis)
holes.what: Aristotle's defense of tragedy and imitation as natural, cathartic, and educational, imparting universal and necessary truths about human life.
holes.why: Chapter 24 needs the Poetics to stage Rear Window as adjudicating Plato's ban on imitative art against Aristotle's claim that drama cultivates moral insight - the film's epiphany about Jeff's neighbors is exactly the Aristotelian payoff.

holes.name: Supererogation (beyond the call of duty)
holes.what: The category of acts that are good to perform but not wrong to omit, as when Jeff's intervention might be praiseworthy without being required.
holes.why: Chapter 25 needs the obligatory/supererogatory distinction to argue that once Jeff knows of Thorwald's crime, intervening is a genuine obligation rather than a merely heroic option.

holes.name: Kinds of Probability (physical, statistical, evidential)
holes.what: The philosophical distinction between physical, statistical, and evidential probability - different senses in which an event can be improbable and different ways evidence supports a theory.
holes.why: Chapter 27's entire analysis of Hitchcock plot twists and of Jeff-and-Doyle's evidence assessment in Rear Window turns on keeping these three kinds of improbability apart.

holes.name: Intentionalism, New Criticism and Subjectivism (meaning in art)
holes.what: Competing theories of artistic interpretation holding that an artwork's meaning is fixed by the artist's intention, by the work itself, or by audience reception.
holes.why: Chapter 28 uses Hitchcock's cameos as its test case, arguing each of the three theories holds within its own domain and that no single source exhausts artistic meaning.

holes.name: The Problem of Other Minds
holes.what: The puzzle of how we can know that other people have conscious minds rather than being unfeeling automata, given that we observe only their behavior.
holes.why: Chapter 30 offers Shadow of a Doubt as a counterexample to the Cartesian other-minds skepticism Descartes motivates with his hats-and-coats passage, with the two Charlies knowing each other's minds.
